security_spec.violation_condition: In XiangShan IOPMP RTL, the wired interrupt output signal (iopmp_intr) and MSI write trigger are generated in the same cycle when MSI is enabled (err_cfg.msi_en=1 and imp_msi=1). The spec mandates mutual exclusion: wired interrupt must be deasserted when MSI is triggered. If the RTL's interrupt generation logic uses independent combinational paths for wired interrupt and MSI without proper mutual-exclusion gating, both fire simultaneously — a double-interrupt. Additionally, if the MSI write-error sticky bit (err_info.msi_werr) is not properly sampled and held across cycles, the RTL could re-attempt failed MSI writes indefinitely, flooding the system bus.
security_spec.vulnerability_pattern: assign io_intrpt = ie & ~suppress & ~msi_en; assign msi_trigger = ie & ~suppress & msi_en & ~msi_werr; // mutual exclusion missing or glitch-prone
security_spec.summary: Wired interrupt and MSI generation must be mutually exclusive in hardware; simultaneous assertion causes duplicate interrupt delivery and potential MSI write-error DoS loop

findings.finding: Wired interrupt (io.int) is generated combinatorially from errinfo_v, errcfg_ie, and per-entry sire/siwe suppression attributes. There is zero reference to err_cfg.msi_en in this block — no '& ~msi_en' mutual-exclusion term. When MSI support is added in the future, both wired interrupt and MSI write will fire simultaneously, producing the exact double-interrupt DoS described in the vulnerability pattern.

The Ctrl FSM has 9 states (sIdle through sDone) for the check pipeline. No state exists for MSI write transaction initiation, address handshake, data handshake, response capture, or msi_werr error recording. The entire MSI delivery path has no FSM backbone to sequence bus writes.

Ctrl module outputs only int, flush, rs, enable. No MSI write request, MSI address bus, MSI data bus, or MSI write-complete input ports exist. There is no hardware path from the error-capture FSM to any bus master interface that could issue an MSI write.
findings.snippet:
val stall = Input(Bool())
val int = Output(Bool())
val flush = Output(Bool())
val rs = Output(Bool())
val enable = Output(Bool())

findings.finding: RegErrmsiaddr and RegErrmsiaddrh class definitions exist only inside a /* not implemented ... not implemented end */ comment block (line ~601-616). These registers are never instantiated in RegMap. No MSI target address can be configured, making MSI mode non-functional even if software sets msi_en=1.

The write-1-clear handler for ERR_INFO.msi_werr is commented out. Spec (RegErrinfo line 663 comment) mandates R/W1C behavior — software must be able to clear msi_werr by writing 1. With the handler disabled, msi_werr would be permanently sticky if any hardware logic ever set it to 1, forcing software into an unrecoverable state.

ERR_INFO.msi_werr (bit 3) is declared as a spec-mandated field that 'is asserted when the write access to trigger an IOPMP-originated MSI has failed.' However, a grep across the entire Ctrl module body (lines 1003-1329) returns zero hits for 'msi'. No hardware logic ever drives msi_werr to 1. The field is permanently 0 regardless of MSI write outcomes. Software reading ERR_INFO would see msi_werr=0 even if a hypothetical MSI write failed — a silent error.
findings.snippet:
init_val.msi_werr := IopmpParams.msi_werr.U // 0.U
...
val msi_werr = UInt(1.W)  // [R/W1C] It's asserted when the write access to trigger an IOPMP-originated MSI has failed.

findings.finding: msi_en and msidata are exported from RegMap into the RegMapIO bundle (wired at line 753-754 as Output fields) and connected to Ctrl's reg input port (line 1016: Flipped(new RegMapIO)). The Ctrl module reads the entire RegMapIO bundle but never references its msi_en or msidata sub-fields — they are dead wire connections. Software can write msi_en=1 via APB but the hardware Ctrl ignores the value entirely.

ERR_CFG.msi_en initializes to IopmpParams.msi_en which is 0 (line 53: val msi_en = 0), but the inline comment reads '// 1.U'. This misleading comment could cause a developer to believe MSI is enabled by default at reset. The actual hardware correctly defaults to wired interrupt mode (msi_en=0).

RegHwcfg2 Bundle declares prio_entry and rrid_transl fields but has no msi_en capability/advertise field. Software has no standard way to discover whether the hardware supports MSI delivery. The IopmpParams.msi_en default is 0, which is correct (MSI not supported), but if MSI were added, the hwcfg register must advertise it.

The Ctrl module's output logic has four independent combinational paths: io.int (line 1307-1318), io.rs (line 1324), io.flush (line 1321), io.enable (line 1327). There is no Mux, priority encoder, or gating network that selects between wired interrupt assertion vs. MSI write trigger based on msi_en. The architectural precondition for the double-interrupt bug is already baked into the design — adding an MSI FSM without also gating the wired interrupt path guarantees simultaneous firing.
